overview: Then this Commercial Driving License (CDL) Entry Level Driver Training (ELDT) – Class A course is the perfect next step. Created to help you build the skills and confidence needed to operate large combination vehicles safely, this training covers everything from vehicle inspections and coupling procedures to shifting, backing, and on-road driving techniques. It fully aligns with FMCSA and DOT regulations in 49 CFR Part 380, ensuring you meet all federal ELDT requirements as you work toward your Class A commercial license.
To obtain your Class A Endorsement Training certificate, you must pass the final exam with 80% or more.
audience: Individuals who plan to operate combination vehicles with a GCWR of 26,001 pounds or more when towing a trailer over 10,000 pounds.
Drivers seeking employment in long-haul or regional trucking.
Operators of tractor-trailers, semi-trucks, and big rigs.
Workers transporting heavy loads for industries such as freight, logistics, construction, and agriculture.
New drivers who must meet FMCSA ELDT requirements.

Behind-the-Wheel (BTW) Training: Some states may also require BTW training in addition to this course. syllabus.intro: This Class A CDL Training online course consists of 30 lessons categorized under five modules. Students are required to take each lesson in sequential order as listed below.

modules.title: Module 1: Basic Operation of a Commercial Motor Vehicle
modules.desc: This module will give driver-trainees a fundamental understanding of Class A Commercial Motor Vehicles (CMV) and their operation. The focus will be on familiarizing trainees with the essential instruments, controls, and operating characteristics of CMV. Additionally, this module will cover essential topics such as Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations (FMCSR), vehicle inspections, vehicle control, shifting and backing techniques, and coupling and uncoupling procedures.

modules.title: Module 2: Safe Operating Procedures
modules.desc: This module will focus on the safe operation of combination vehicles on highways under various roads, weather, and traffic conditions. Trainees will learn essential practices for navigating different driving environments and adhering to Federal regulations. A key component of this module will be instruction on the proper use of seat belt assemblies, as mandated by 49 CFR Section 392.16 of the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations, which states, "No driver shall operate a commercial motor vehicle, and a motor carrier shall not require or permit a driver to operate a commercial motor vehicle, that has a seat belt assembly installed at the driver's seat unless the seat belt assembly properly restrains the driver."

modules.title: Module 3: Advanced Operating Practices
modules.desc: This module will build upon the foundational skills and knowledge acquired in Modules 1 and 2. Trainees will delve into advanced driving techniques essential for recognizing and effectively responding to potential hazards on the road. Drivers will also learn the skills required to handle CMVs in challenging and hazardous situations and ensure safe operation.
lessons: Lesson 16: Skid Control, Recovery, Jackknifing, and Other Emergencies

modules.title: Module 4: Vehicle Systems and Reporting Malfunctions
modules.desc: This module will give driver-trainees a comprehensive understanding of combination vehicles, including their systems and subsystems. The goal is to equip trainees with the knowledge necessary to appreciate the importance of vehicle inspection, operation, and maintenance in ensuring highway safety and operational efficiency.
lessons: Lesson 18: Identification and Diagnosis of Malfunctions

modules.title: Module 5: Non-Driving Activities
modules.desc: This module will focus on essential non-driving activities for a CMV's safe and efficient operation.

objectives: Understand the components of a combination vehicle, key safety fundamentals, and regulatory requirements, including the consequences of non-compliance with FMCSA regulations.
Identify and use vehicle instruments, controls, and safety components, including proper use of safety belts and mirrors.
Perform pre-trip, post-trip, and en route inspections, ensuring compliance with regulatory standards.
Demonstrate basic vehicle control, including executing turns, centering the vehicle, and maneuvering in restricted areas.
Proficiently execute shifting maneuvers, demonstrating safe and efficient operation of multi-speed dual range transmissions.
Safely back and dock combination vehicles, utilizing techniques such as "Get Out and Look" (GOAL) and spotter assistance.
Execute safe coupling and uncoupling procedures for combination vehicle units.
Apply safe driving practices under various road, weather, and traffic conditions, including effective use of seat belts.
Recognize and respond to potential hazards in the driving environment, emphasizing hazard recognition and emergency preparedness.
Identify causes of skidding and jackknifing and apply techniques for avoiding and recovering from these situations.
Ensure safe and efficient cargo handling, securement, and documentation, understanding the importance of cargo security.
Develop effective trip planning skills, including route selection, rest stop planning, and compliance with vehicle size and weight limitations.
faqs: What training and testing are required to earn a CDL Class A license training Endorsement?

A Commercial Driver's License (CDL) is required to operate a Commercial Motor Vehicle (CMV). A CMV is any vehicle used for commerce that meets specific criteria, such as having a gross vehicle weight rating of at least 26,001 pounds or being designed to transport 16 or more passengers, including the driver.

To obtain a Class A Commercial Driver's License (CDL), drivers must follow several steps and meet specific eligibility requirements.

Eligibility Requirements:

- Must meet the minimum age requirement set by the State.

- Must hold a valid driver’s license.

- Must provide proof of U.S. citizenship or legal residency.

- Must pass a medical examination and obtain a Medical Examiner’s Certificate, verifying physical fitness to operate a CMV.

Step 1: Obtain a Commercial Learner’s Permit (CLP)

- Pass the required knowledge tests to obtain a CLP.

- With a CLP, practice driving a Class A CMV under the supervision of a qualified CDL holder.

Step 2: Complete Training and Practice

- Complete required training programs such as this ELDT Class A Training course.

- Gain hands-on experience driving a Class A CMV.

Step 3: Pass the CDL Knowledge Test and Skills Test

- Take the General Knowledge Test and pass as defined in 49 CFR Part 380.

- Demonstrate a thorough understanding of vehicle inspection procedures.

- Show proficiency in controlling the vehicle through various maneuvers.

- Prove the ability to operate a Class A CMV on public roads.

Step 4: Obtain the Class A CDL

- Once all requirements are met, apply for and receive your Class A CDL.

- Check with your State’s Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) or licensing agency for any additional requirements or procedures.
Do I also need Behind-the-Wheel training?

This course satisfies the ELDT theory training requirement for the knowledge test. However, many states require students to also complete Behind-the-Wheel (BTW) training with a registered training provider before taking the CDL skills test. BTW training is not included in this course and must be completed separately if required by your state.

Approved Behind-the-Wheel training providers can be found through your state Driver Licensing Agency, such as the state DMV or DOT, or through the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration’s Training Provider Registry (TPR). These resources list training providers authorized to deliver the required ELDT Behind-the-Wheel training.
Why is the ELDT – Class A course important?

The Class A CDL Training course holds significant importance for various reasons.

- It equips drivers with the knowledge and skills necessary to operate large commercial vehicles safely, reducing the risk of accidents and improving road safety.

- It ensures that drivers meet Federal requirements set by the FMCSA, which helps maintain consistent standards across the industry.

- The course covers essential topics such as vehicle operation, safety protocols, and regulatory compliance, which are fundamental for handling Class A vehicles effectively.

- It helps drivers meet the industry’s standards for professionalism and competence, which can enhance their employability and career prospects.

- It provides comprehensive training that builds drivers' confidence in their ability to manage complex driving situations and handle large vehicles safely.
Which regulations are covered by this Class A CDL training course?

The course meets and exceeds the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) compliance requirements and the United States Department of Transportation’s (DOT’s) Regulations as defined in 49 CFR Part 380.
Are there any prerequisites for enrolling in the ELDT Class A course?

Before beginning your training, you will need to meet specific prerequisites. These may include:

- Being at least 18 (21 years old to drive across state lines).

- Hold a valid driver’s license (not a commercial one) in the state where you plan to be trained.

- Passing a Department of Transportation (DOT) physical exam and drug screen.

- Meeting any additional requirements set by the training provider or state licensing agency.
Is the ELDT Class A course recognized by all American States?

Yes! The State of Washington requires classroom instruction by a registered Washington Training Provider for all types of CDL certifications and endorsements. These requirements apply only to drivers who hold a Washington license or are obtaining a Washington CDL.
How will the FMCSA know that I have completed and passed this CDL Class A license training?

This ensures that your training records are updated and accessible to the FMCSA, verifying that you have met the necessary requirements.

Once this is done, you are eligible to take your State's Class A knowledge test. Successfully passing the knowledge test will qualify you to receive the Class A CDL.
Is this ELDT Class A the only training I need to get my CDL Class A license?

No. You must pass a medical exam to ensure you are physically qualified to operate a commercial vehicle. This test must be conducted by a professional listed on the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration's (FMCSA) National Registry of Certified Medical Examiners.

You must also complete this online CDL ELDT Class A theory course before taking the State Class A Knowledge Exam, which is typically administered at the state motor vehicle office. Department of Transportation's (DOT) Training Provider Registry (TPR). Once this is done, you are eligible to take your State's Class A knowledge test. Following the knowledge test, you must pass a skills test that includes both a pre-trip inspection and a driving test.

Obtaining a Class A CDL may require passing a Federally required background check. It is essential to check with your local Department of Motor Vehicles or Motor Vehicles Division office if this is necessary.

modules.title: Module 1: Hazmat Basic Requirements and Communication
modules.desc: This module sets the stage for understanding the rules and regulations governing hazardous materials transportation. This includes understanding the hazardous materials table; proper marking, labeling, and placarding of hazardous materials cargo, and the preparation and importance of shipping papers. This module will also explain how to identify the appropriate reporting channels in emergencies involving hazardous materials.
lessons: Lesson 1: Basic Introductory Hazardous Materials Requirements
Lesson 3: Reporting Hazardous Materials Crashes and Releases

modules.title: Module 2: Safe Transportation Practices
modules.desc: This module introduces practical procedures for safely transporting hazardous materials. You will learn how to safely navigate tunnels and railroad crossings by following specific regulations. This module also covers proper loading and unloading techniques for hazardous materials, ensuring cargo is segregated, secured, and meets regulations for transport alongside foodstuffs.
lessons: Lesson 4: Tunnels and Railroad (RR)-Highway Grade Crossing Requirements
Lesson 5: Loading and Unloading Hazardous Materials
Lesson 6: Hazardous Materials on Passenger Vehicles

You will learn the proper procedures for reporting incidents and implementing best practices for emergency response. The focus will be on protecting people, property, and the environment.

modules.title: Module 4: Pre-Trip and Operational Considerations
modules.desc: Module 4 emphasizes the importance of pre-trip checks for safe transportation of hazardous materials. You will learn the proper procedures for checking vehicle tires before each trip. faqs: What are the training and testing requirements for obtaining a CDL with a Hazardous Materials (H) Endorsement?

To operate a Commercial Motor Vehicle (CMV), you must have a valid Commercial Driver’s License (CDL). A CMV includes vehicles used for commerce with a gross vehicle weight rating of 26,001 pounds or more, or those designed to carry 16 or more passengers (excluding the driver).

To earn a CDL, all applicants must pass both a knowledge test and a skills test. While everyone must take the General Knowledge Test, drivers applying for the Hazardous Materials (H) Endorsement must also pass the required ELDT Hazmat Endorsement knowledge test as defined in 49 CFR 383.5. Additionally, applicants must complete a TSA background check as part of the hazmat clearance process.

After completing the hazmat knowledge test, drivers must take the standard CDL skills tests, which include:

- Vehicle inspection

- Basic vehicle control

- On-road driving

These tests must be taken in the same type of vehicle the applicant plans to be licensed for. Vehicles with components that are marked or labeled cannot be used for the Vehicle Inspection Test.

Drivers who plan to transport liquid or gaseous materials in tanks with an individual capacity of more than 119 gallons, and a combined capacity of 1,000 gallons or more, whether permanently or temporarily attached to the vehicle, must also pass the Tank Vehicle (N) Endorsement test as required by FMCSA.
Why is the CDL Entry Level Driver Training (ELDT) - HAZMAT (H) Endorsement course important?

The CDL Entry Level Driver Training (ELDT) - HAZMAT (H) Endorsement course holds significant importance for various reasons.

- It equips drivers with the knowledge and skills to safely transport hazardous materials, reducing the risk of accidents and protecting themselves, the public, and the environment.

- It ensures drivers comply with federal regulations governing the transport of hazardous materials, avoiding fines and potential license suspension.

- It qualifies drivers to haul hazardous materials, opening doors to new job opportunities.

- The ELDT Hazmat Endorsement demonstrates a driver's commitment to safety and specialized knowledge in handling hazardous materials.

- Accidents involving hazardous materials can be catastrophic, resulting in hefty fines, clean-up costs, and potential lawsuits. Proper training can help prevent these incidents, saving companies significant expenses in the long run.
Which regulations are covered by the CDL Entry Level Driver Training (ELDT) - HAZMAT (H) Endorsement course?

The course meets and exceeds the compliance requirements of the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) and the United States Department of Transportation’s (DOT’s) Hazardous Material Regulations (HMR; 49 CFR Parts 171-180).
Is refresher training required for the CDL Entry Level Driver Training (ELDT) - HAZMAT (H) Endorsement course?

According to the rules of the FMCSA, there is no need to take a refresher training for this ELDT Hazmat Endorsement training as it is aimed as a first-time training for entry-level drivers.

However, the DOT regulations mandate that all personnel involved in the transportation process of hazardous materials must receive refresher/retaining once every three years.
Are there any prerequisites for enrolling in the CDL Entry Level Driver Training (ELDT) - HAZMAT (H) Endorsement course?
This program is designed for drivers seeking to apply to add an (H) endorsement to an existing CDL, hence participants should be at least 18 years old and hold a valid commercial driver’s license.
Is the CDL Entry Level Driver Training (ELDT) - HAZMAT (H) Endorsement course recognized by all American States?

Yes! The state of Washington requires classroom instruction by a registered Washington Training Provider for all kinds of CDL certifications and endorsements. These requirements apply only to drivers who hold a Washington license or are obtaining a Washington CDL.

- Commercial Drivers who may be tasked with transporting hazmat;

- Tanker Truck Drivers,

- Hazmat Material Haulers (Liquid/Gas),

- Hazmat Drivers for Energy Companies,

- Hazmat Waste Transporters, and

- Hazmat Drivers in specialized industries such as explosives in the mining sector or radioactive materials in the medical field.

This ensures that your training records are updated and accessible to the FMCSA, verifying that you have met the necessary requirements.

Once this is done, you are eligible to take your state's hazmat knowledge test. Successfully passing the knowledge test will qualify you to receive the H endorsement.

faqs: What is a CDL Entry Level Driver Training (ELDT) - Tanker (N) Endorsement?

A Tanker (N) endorsement is an added qualification on your CDL that confirms you understand how to safely operate vehicles carrying large volumes of liquid or gas. This includes loads ranging from food products such as milk and juice to fuels and industrial liquids, including gasoline, whether the tanks are permanently or temporarily attached to the vehicle or chassis.
When is an ELDT Tanker (N) endorsement required?

You are required to hold a tanker (N) endorsement if the vehicle you operate meets the federal definition of a tank vehicle. This includes any vehicle with a single tank of 119 gallons or more, or multiple tanks with a combined capacity of 1,000 gallons or more. This requirement does not apply only to traditional tanker trucks; drivers hauling large liquid totes or IBCs on flatbeds or in dry vans may also meet this definition and need this CDL endorsement.
What are the training and testing requirements for obtaining a CDL Entry Level Driver Training (ELDT) - Tanker (N) Endorsement?

To obtain a CDL with a Tanker (N) Endorsement, drivers must meet the following training and testing requirements:

- Hold a valid CDL permit for the appropriate vehicle class (Class A, B, or C).

- Complete FMCSA-compliant Entry-Level Driver Training (ELDT) covering CDL Tanker (N) endorsement training online.

- Pass the CDL Tanker Vehicle (N) knowledge test at the state DMV.

- Comply with all federal and state-specific requirements, including age, medical certification, and driving eligibility standards.

Once these requirements are met, the driver is issued the N endorsement, authorizing the transportation of bulk tanks.
Which regulations are covered by the CDL Entry Level Driver Training (ELDT) - Tanker (N) Endorsement Training?

FMCSA requires records of course training only for Class A, B, and C licenses, and for the H (Hazardous Materials), P (Passenger), and S (School Bus) endorsements. The N (Tank Vehicle) endorsement does not require FMCSA-reported training.

To obtain the N endorsement, drivers must take the tank vehicle knowledge test at their state DMV. A passing score of 80% results in the N endorsement being stamped on your CDL.

faqs: What training and testing are required to obtain a School Bus (S) Endorsement under ELDT requirements?

Individuals enrolling in ELDT School Bus (S) Endorsement training must already hold a valid Commercial Learner’s Permit (CLP) or Commercial Driver’s License (CDL) of the appropriate class—Class B or Class C, depending on the type of school bus they will operate.

A CDL is required for anyone operating a Commercial Motor Vehicle (CMV). CMVs include vehicles used for commerce with a gross vehicle weight rating of 26,001 pounds or more, or vehicles designed to transport 16 or more passengers, including the driver.

To obtain a CDL, all applicants must pass both a knowledge test and a skills test. Everyone must take the General Knowledge Test, but drivers seeking the School Bus (S) Endorsement must also pass the required ELDT School Bus endorsement knowledge test. After successfully completing the knowledge tests, applicants must take the CDL skills tests, which include:

- Vehicle inspection

- Basic vehicle control

- On-road driving

These skills tests must be taken in the same type of school bus the driver intends to be licensed for. Vehicles with marked or labeled components cannot be used for the Vehicle Inspection Test.
Do I also need Behind-the-Wheel training?

This course satisfies the ELDT theory training requirement for the knowledge test. However, many states require students to also complete Behind-the-Wheel (BTW) training with a registered training provider before taking the CDL skills test. BTW training is not included in this course and must be completed separately if required by your state.

Approved Behind-the-Wheel training providers can be found through your state Driver Licensing Agency, such as the state DMV or DOT, or through the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration’s Training Provider Registry (TPR). These resources list training providers authorized to deliver the required ELDT Behind-the-Wheel training.
Why is the CDL Entry Level Driver Training (ELDT) - School Bus (S) Endorsement course important?

Here are some key reasons why obtaining the school bus endorsement is important:

- Specialized Training: The endorsement requires drivers to complete a comprehensive training program that covers topics such as: Safety regulations: Understanding and complying with federal and state laws pertaining to school bus operations.

- Emergency procedures: Knowing how to handle emergency situations like accidents, medical emergencies, and hazardous materials incidents.

- Student management: Learning effective strategies for interacting with students and maintaining a safe and positive environment.

- Vehicle inspection: Understanding the importance of pre-trip and post-trip inspections to identify potential safety hazards.
- Legal Requirement: Many jurisdictions require commercial drivers to have a school bus endorsement in order to legally transport students.

- Increased Responsibility: School bus drivers are responsible for the safety of young passengers. The endorsement demonstrates that they have the necessary skills and knowledge to fulfill this important role.
Which regulations are covered by the CDL Entry Level Driver Training (ELDT) - School Bus (S) Endorsement course?

The course meets and exceeds the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) compliance requirements and the United States Department of Transportation’s (DOT’s) Regulations defined in 49 CFR Part 605.
Is refresher training required for the CDL Entry Level Driver Training (ELDT) - School Bus (S) Endorsement course?
Most school bus drivers need some form of refresher training every year, and a more complete skills or compliance refresher every 3–5 years, depending on their local regulations.
Are there any prerequisites for enrolling in the CDL Entry Level Driver Training (ELDT) - School Bus (S) Endorsement course?

This ELDT training for school bus drivers typically requires a valid Class B or C Commercial Driver's License (CDL) and a clean driving record before pursuing the certification.

Generally, individuals must be at least 21 years old to obtain a CDL with a school bus endorsement, though minimum age requirements can vary by State. Some States may have different age requirements for various types of CDLs or endorsements. Therefore, always check with your State's licensing agency for specific age requirements and other regulations.
Is the CDL Entry Level Driver Training (ELDT) - School Bus (S) Endorsement course recognized by all American States?

Yes! The State of Washington requires classroom instruction by a registered Washington Training Provider for all types of CDL certifications and endorsements. These requirements apply only to drivers who hold a Washington license or are obtaining a Washington CDL.
Who would benefit from enrolling in the CDL Entry Level Driver Training (ELDT) - School Bus (S) Endorsement course?

Individuals interested in pursuing a career as a school bus driver or those required to obtain a School Bus (S) Endorsement on their Commercial Driver's License (CDL) can follow this course. The following individuals would benefit from enrolling in this course:

- Aspiring school bus drivers,

- Current CDL holders who need to add the School Bus (S) Endorsement to their license to expand their job opportunities,

- School district employees such as transportation coordinators or substitute drivers must drive a school bus occasionally and require proper certification,

- Employees or prospective employees of private or charter bus companies that provide school transportation services,

- Individuals who have previously driven a school bus but have been out of the field for some time must update their skills and meet current regulatory requirements, or

- State and local government employees who operate school buses as part of their job duties for State or local governments.

overview: The OSHA 10-Hour Construction course is an introductory, online safety training program aligned with the requirements codified in OSHA Standards 29 CFR 1926. Designed for entry-level construction industry workers who need a strong foundation in workplace safety and health. This OSHA 10-hour construction training helps workers become more knowledgeable about common job-related hazards and proven best practices to prevent or minimize injuries and incidents on construction sites.

Through this online training, participants learn how to recognize, avoid, abate, and prevent workplace hazards commonly found in construction environments. The course also explains worker rights, employer responsibilities, and proper procedures for filing a safety or health complaint, supporting a safer and more compliant jobsite culture.

This program is voluntary and does not satisfy the training requirements of any specific OSHA standard. However, many states, local jurisdictions, employers, and labor unions require OSHA 10-hour construction training to meet internal safety policies or contractual obligations.
Upon successful completion, participants receive an official U.S. Department of Labor (DOL) card.
OSHA Outreach courses are provided in partnership with ClickSafety, an OSHA-authorized online Outreach Training provider.

overview: HAZWOPER training course provides 40 hours of training that covers the OSHA Hazardous Waste Operations and Emergency Response (HAZWOPER) standards, for compliance with OSHA 29 CFR 1910.120(e) and 29 CFR 1926.65(e) regulations. The purpose of the course is to prepare workers involved in cleanup and emergency response operations to work safely in situations involving hazardous substances. The training includes policies, practices, and procedures that help reduce the risk of injury and illness due to harmful exposure on the job.
audience: equipment operators
general laborers

syllabus.intro: The OSHA 40 Hour HAZWOPER Training course consists of 18 modules broken down into 80 hazardous materials and emergency response lessons. Students are required to take each lesson in sequential order as listed below.

modules.title: Module 1: Regulatory Overview
modules.desc: Module 1 covers OSHA and HAZWOPER standards for the general industry (29 CFR 1910.120) and for the construction industry (29 CFR 1926.65), in addition to relevant NFPA and DOT information.
lessons: Lesson 1: OSHA and the HAZWOPER Standard
Lesson 3: NFPA System and DOT Labels

modules.title: Module 2: Planning and Organization
modules.desc: The organizational structure of a hazardous waste site is important because it determines how tasks are assigned and how communication flows. The site safety and health plan is important because it outlines the procedures that will be used to protect workers from hazards. The organizational structure of a hazardous waste site will vary depending on the size and complexity of the site. However, there are some common elements that are found in all organizational structures.
lessons: Lesson 5: Site Safety and Health Plan

modules.title: Module 3: Site Characterization
modules.desc: HAZWOPER Site Characterization is the process of gathering information about a hazardous waste site in order to identify and assess the hazards present at the site. This information is used to develop a Site Safety and Health Plan (SSHP) and to implement safe work practices.

modules.title: Module 4: Medical Surveillance
modules.desc: HAZWOPER Medical Surveillance is a program that is designed to monitor the health of workers who are exposed to hazardous waste. The goal of the program is to identify any health problems that may be caused by exposure to hazardous waste, and to take steps to prevent or treat those problems.

modules.title: Module 5: Toxicology
modules.desc: This knowledge can be used to develop safe work practices, to prevent exposure to hazardous waste, and to treat people who have been exposed to hazardous waste.
lessons: Lesson 14: Chemicals and Target Organ Toxicity

modules.title: Module 6: Hazard Classification
modules.desc: HAZWOPER Hazard Classification is a system for classifying hazardous waste materials based on their physical and chemical properties. The system is used to identify the hazards posed by hazardous waste materials, and to develop safe work practices to protect workers and the environment.

modules.title: Module 7: Chemical Hazards
modules.desc: Chemical hazards are one of the most common hazards associated with hazardous waste. These hazards can be caused by the properties of the waste itself, or by the way the waste is handled.

modules.title: Module 8: Radiological Hazards
modules.desc: Radiological hazards are one of the most serious hazards associated with hazardous waste. Radioactive materials can cause cancer, birth defects, and other health problems. They can also damage property and the environment. The hazards posed by radioactive waste can vary depending on the specific waste. It is important to be aware of the hazards associated with any radioactive waste that you are working with.

modules.title: Module 9: Respiratory Protection
modules.desc: Respiratory protection is one of the most important aspects of HAZWOPER compliance. Respirators can protect workers from exposure to harmful airborne contaminants, such as asbestos, lead, and mercury. There are a number of different types of respirators available, each with its own advantages and disadvantages. The type of respirator that is best for a particular situation will depend on the specific hazards that are present.

modules.title: Module 10: Personal Protective Equipment
modules.desc: Module 10 examines the importance of chemical protective clothing (CPC) and PPE for the eyes, ears, hands, and feet when working in certain HazMat environments.
lessons: Lesson 37: PPE for the Head, Eyes, Face and Ears
Lesson 38: PPE for the Hands and Feet
Lesson 39: Selection of Chemical Protective Clothing
Lesson 40: Monitoring and Medical Concerns of PPE
Lesson 42: Inspection and Maintenance of PPE

modules.title: Module 11: Decontamination
modules.desc: Decontamination is the process of removing or neutralizing contaminants that have accumulated on personnel and equipment. It is a critical part of hazardous waste operations and emergency response. The purpose of decontamination is to protect workers and the environment from the hazards of hazardous waste. Contaminated workers can spread hazardous materials to other areas, and contaminated equipment can release hazardous materials into the environment.

modules.title: Module 12: Air Monitoring
modules.desc: Air monitoring is the process of measuring the concentration of hazardous substances in the air. It is an important part of hazardous waste operations and emergency response. The purpose of air monitoring is to identify and quantify airborne hazards, so that appropriate protective measures can be implemented. Air monitoring can also be used to assess the effectiveness of remediation efforts.

modules.title: Module 13: Compressed Gases
modules.desc: Module 13 surveys the nature of compressed gas cylinders and includes information on proper handling, transportation, and emergency response.
lessons: Lesson 56: Safe Handling and Storage of Cylinders
Lesson 57: Transportation and Disposal of Cylinders

modules.title: Module 14: Material Sampling and Analysis
modules.desc: Module 14 covers various types of sampling plans for use with toxic or hazardous substances on a HazMat worksite.

modules.title: Module 15: Handling Drums
modules.desc: Module 15 instructs learners on the proper methods for opening, transporting, and sampling drums of hazardous waste or other toxic or hazardous substances.
lessons: Lesson 63: Opening Various Types of Drums

modules.title: Module 16: Confined Spaces
modules.desc: Module 16 covers roles, entry procedures, safety protocols, and emergency response for confined spaces on a HazMat work site.
lessons: Lesson 67: Confined Space Roles and Responsibilities
Lesson 73: Confined Space Rescue and Emergencies

modules.title: Module 17: Excavations
modules.desc: Module 17 covers excavations on a hazardous waste site, paying special attention to soil classification and the correct use of protective systems.

modules.title: Module 18: Emergency Response Procedures
modules.desc: Module 18 discusses emergency response measures, first responder considerations, and fire service involvement at a HAZWOPER worksite.

faqs: Which Federal OSHA standards are covered by the OSHA 40-Hour HAZWOPER Training?

The course meets and exceeds the compliance requirements of OSHA 29 CFR 1910.120(e) and 29 CFR 1926.65(e) regulations.

The OSHA 40 Hour HAZWOPER certification covers the General Site Clean-up provision.
What is the difference between the OSHA 40-Hour and 24-Hour HAZWOPER Training certificate courses?

The OSHA 40-Hour HAZWOPER Training course targets workers exposed to contaminated substances that exceed the Permissible Exposure Limits (PELs) and, hence, must wear the appropriate personal protective equipment.

The OSHA 24-Hour HAZWOPER Training course targets workers working at contaminated sites but undertaking tasks that do not expose them to hazardous substances at or above the PELs.
What type of employees require the OSHA 40-Hour HAZWOPER Training certificate?

The OSHA 40-Hour HAZWOPER certification is required for workers who are involved in handling hazardous waste operations and emergency response. This includes but is not limited to employees engaged in cleaning up hazardous waste sites, handling and disposing of hazardous waste, and responding to hazardous materials spills.

- Workers who handle contaminated waste, soil, water, etc.

- Workers who handle tanks that store/treat pipes that pump in/out contaminated waste.

- Workers who may work near sites that release contaminated waste.

- Workers who may work near contaminated sites, such as hazardous waste treatment plants.

- Clean-up operations crews of hazardous waste sites.

- Workers with emergency response teams who handle or may be exposed to contaminated substances.

- Workers who work at a listed or proposed listing site under the Superfund National Priority List (NPL).

- Workers who conduct operations at corrective action sites under the purview of U.S. EPA's Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA).

You can refresh your HAZWOPER certification by taking the OSHA 8-Hour HAZWOPER Refresher Training course.

The 40-hour HAZWOPER training can be done online.

faqs: What is the duration of the HAZWOPER Refresher Training course?

The HAZWOPER Refresher Training course will take around 8 hours to complete. However, since the course is largely self-paced, the exact training time will vary based on how quickly learners progress through the material.
Are there any prerequisites to taking the HAZWOPER Refresher course?

Yes. OSHA requires all workers involved in hazardous waste operations to first complete an initial OSHA 24 or 40 Hour HAZWOPER Training. After this initial training, workers must complete an OSHA 8 Hour HAZWOPER Refresher Training course each year to maintain their certification and receive updates on important regulatory changes.
How often must the OSHA 8 Hour HAZWOPER Refresher Training be taken?
The OSHA 8 Hour HAZWOPER Refresher Training course must be taken every 12 months to maintain current OSHA 24 Hour or 40 Hour HAZWOPER Training certifications.
Can I receive a first-time OSHA 24-Hour or 40 Hour HAZWOPER certification by completing the OSHA 8 Hour HAZWOPER Refresher Training course?

No. The OSHA 8 Hour HAZWOPER Refresher Training is a refresher course for the OSHA 24 Hour or 40 Hour HAZWOPER certifications. For first-time certification, either the OSHA 24 Hour or 40 Hour HAZWOPER Training courses and necessary field experiences must be completed.
Do I receive a training certificate on completion of the OSHA 8 Hour HAZWOPER Refresher Training?
Yes, a certificate will be sent once the course is successfully completed.
What to do if the OSHA 8-Hour HAZWOPER Refresher training isn't received in 12 months?

According to OSHA, “If the date for refresher training has lapsed, the need to repeat the initial training must be determined based on the employee’s familiarity with safety and health procedures used on site. The employee should take the next available refresher training course. There should be a record in the employee’s file indicating why the training has been delayed and when the training will be completed.”
In terms of the OSHA 8 Hour HAZWOPER Refresher Training, does OSHA accept computer-based training?

According to OSHA, “Computer-based training may meet some refresher training requirements, provided that it covers topics relevant to workers’ assigned duties. It must be supplemented by the opportunity to ask questions of a qualified trainer and by an assessment of the hands-on performance of work tasks.”
Is it possible to split up the OSHA 8 Hour HAZWOPER Refresher Training into segments?
According to OSHA, “Refresher training may be given in segments so long as the required 8 hours have been completed by the employee’s anniversary date.”

overview: Your facility may have witnessed a tanker truck accident on the highway or a rail car leaking an unknown chemical on the loading dock. During the first few minutes after the accident, the responding individual is not there to intervene; they are there to identify the hazard, isolate the area, and notify the appropriate individuals to prevent injury. That is where this course fills the gap. It makes the difference between an innocent bystander and an effective first responder in those critical first few minutes.

This 4-hour course fulfills OSHA HAZWOPER awareness-level training requirements as described in 29 CFR 1910.120(q)(6)(i), and 1926.65(q)(6)(i) covering hazard recognition, notification procedures, and isolation distances. Based on the Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG 2024), learners are taught how to identify placards, read guide numbers, and determine isolation distances.

This course meets and exceeds the compliance requirements outlined in the OSHA HAZWOPER Standard in 29 CFR 1910.120(q)(6)(i) and 1926.65(q)(6)(i) covering hazard recognition, notification procedures, and isolation distances. It also covers the Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG 2024).
Why is the OSHA 4-Hour HAZWOPER First Responder Awareness Level Training important?

This First Responder Awareness Level Training is important because it equips first responders with the knowledge to recognize hazardous materials incidents, protect themselves and the public, and take appropriate initial actions. Early hazard recognition and proper scene isolation help reduce injuries, prevent unnecessary exposure, and ensure that specialized hazardous materials response teams are notified promptly.
Who would benefit from enrolling in the Online Training for the First Responder Awareness Level?

First Responder Awareness personnel are often the first to arrive at a hazardous materials incident. Their role is to recognize hazards, maintain a safe distance, and notify the appropriate authorities. They do not stop or control the release.

Examples include:

- Facility employees

- Security personnel

- Maintenance staff

- Transportation workers

- Warehouse personnel

- General employees who may witness or discover a hazardous materials release.
Does this course teach hazardous materials cleanup?
No. Awareness-level personnel are not trained to contain or clean up hazardous materials. The course focuses on recognition, isolation, and notification.
Are transportation emergencies covered?
Yes. The course includes incidents involving highways, railroads, pipelines, cargo facilities, and other transportation systems where hazardous materials may be present.
What is the difference between Awareness Level and Operations Level training?

Awareness-level responders identify hazards and notify the appropriate authorities, while Operations-level responders receive additional training to take defensive actions to protect people, property, and the environment.
Are there any prerequisites for enrolling in First Responder Awareness Level Training course?
There are no prerequisites for this course.

Yes, refresher training is required every 12 months. The OSHA 4-Hour HAZWOPER First Responder Awareness Level Refresher Training course can be taken in accordance with the regulations.

overview: According to statistics, falls account for one-third of all fatalities in the construction industry. The Center for Construction Research and Training (CPWR) reported in its May 2022 Data Bulletin that, between 2018 and 2020, the construction industry in the United States averaged 376 fatal injuries from falls, slips, and trips and 22,900 nonfatal injuries. Many of these falls were from roofs, scaffolds, and ladders.
This OSHA Fall Protection Training course will cover key areas related to fall hazards and the preventive measures required under 29 CFR 1926 Subpart M for the construction industry.

Lessons will also explain the role of anchorage in a PFAS and the considerations for its selection and use. According to OSHA’s Fall Protection Standard for the Construction Industry (29 CFR 1926 Subpart M), any time work is carried out at a height of 6 feet or more, employers must provide adequate fall protection systems, and workers must be trained to use these systems safely and effectively.
Why is the OSHA Fall Protection Safety Training course important?

Proper fall protection training can go a long way toward safeguarding workers' health and safety and protecting them when working at heights. Fall protection training can be categorized into four levels: awareness, authorized user, competent person, and qualified person. According to OSHA, employers are responsible for providing workers exposed to fall hazards with appropriate fall protection training. This fall protection training educates workers to recognize fall hazards and how to minimize them.
Who would benefit from enrolling in the OSHA Fall Protection Safety Training?

- Managers, supervisors, and workers who must work on overhead platforms, elevated workstations, or over dangerous equipment or machinery as part of their job duties.

- Workers who work at heights doing roofing work, leading-edge work, painting, or bricklaying on high walls, or working on walkways and excavations.

There are no prerequisites for this course.

There is no specific requirement under OSHA that requires refresher training for this course. However, many employers and safety professionals still prefer to conduct periodic refresher training, particularly in workplaces where employees work at heights. overview: OSHA Scaffolding Safety Training provides essential knowledge for employees erecting, disassembling, moving, or inspecting scaffolds. The course covers OSHA’s Scaffolds Standard for the Construction Industry (29 CFR 1926 Subpart L). Scaffolding is widely used for elevated work but incorrect use causes falls, electrocution, and collapses. In fact, scaffolding accidents cause thousands of injuries and dozens of deaths annually in the U.S., highlighting the importance of proper scaffolding safety training. This training ensures employees understand hazards, follow safe procedures, and comply with OSHA scaffolding requirements.

The course teaches recognition of scaffold hazards, correct use of scaffolds, and safe work practices. It also prepares participants for scaffolding certification and scaffold competent person training compliance.

In accordance with OSHA regulations, it is the responsibility of employers to guarantee that all employees working on scaffolding receives training from a qualified person. This training should enable employees to identify the potential hazards associated with the specific type of scaffold being utilized and to have a comprehensive understanding of the procedures in place for managing or reducing those hazards.

Why is Scaffolding Safety Training important?

Scaffolds are temporary structures built at elevated levels to perform work safely above ground. Improper use, design flaws, or engineering faults can lead to serious injuries or fatalities from falls, falling objects, electrocution, or scaffold collapses. Scaffolding safety training teaches workers to recognize hazards associated with the type of scaffold being used and apply procedures to control or minimize risks. Employees gain essential skills for safe scaffold erection, inspection, and operation, while ensuring compliance with OSHA scaffolding training standards under 29 CFR 1926 Subpart L. This training also prepares participants for scaffold competent person training, enhancing workplace safety and reducing scaffold-related accidents.
Who should enroll in the OSHA Scaffolding Safety Training course?

This Scaffolding Safety Training course is designed to provide general information and guidelines to employees involved in erecting, dismantling, moving, operating, repairing, maintaining, or inspecting scaffolds in the construction industry.

Safety professionals, project managers, foremen, scaffolding supervisors, and other personnel who work on scaffolds and want to know more about scaffolding safety would also benefit from enrolling in this course.
What are the areas covered by this OSHA Scaffolding Training course for the construction industry?

This course provides a basic understanding of OSHA’s scaffolding regulations as cited in 29 CFR 1926 Subpart L.

The course also examines the hazards associated with working on or around scaffolding, and the general requirements for the safe use of these elevated work platforms.

The training requirements for users, erectors, and dismantlers of scaffolds are also covered.
Are there any prerequisites before enrolling for the OSHA Scaffolding Safety Training course?
No, there are no prerequisites for this course.

overview: While excavating and trenching have a number of important applications (such as in mining, environmental restoration, and exploration), their use in the construction industry is one of the most common. These operations are used in the construction industry for pipe laying, building foundations, utility work, and more.

Working in and around trenching and excavation operations is inherently dangerous. Hazards include cave-ins, exposure to falling loads, electrocutions, oxygen deficiency, falls, and hazardous atmospheres (among many others). As part of a safety and health program, the OSHA excavations and trenching regulations specified in 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P require employers to implement specific practices that will help reduce the risk of on-the-job injuries and illnesses at trenching and excavation sites.

If your job requires you to work in and around excavations and trenches as a part of your job duties, then it is important that you receive additional on-site training from your employer in addition to this OSHA Excavation, Trenching, and Shoring Safety Training course.

faqs: What is the difference between an excavation and a trench?

OSHA defines an excavation as any man-made cut, cavity, trench, or depression in the Earth’s surface formed by earth removal. A trench is defined as a narrow excavation (in relation to its length) made below the surface of the ground. In general, the depth of a trench is greater than its width, but the width of a trench (measured at the bottom) is not greater than 15 feet (4.6 m).
What unique hazards are associated with excavation and trenching work make this course important to take?

Excavation and trenching work present hazards such as cave-ins, exposure to toxic fumes, asphyxiation, falls, and drowning. This course provides insights into identifying and mitigating these specific risks.

The training also improves workplace safety, reduces the risk of injuries and fatalities, and helps employers maintain safer and more compliant excavation and trenching operations.

This course covers preventive strategies for excavation hazards, including the use of protective systems, proper equipment, and adherence to safety regulations. It emphasizes creating a secure work environment for everyone involved

- Individuals who wish to refresh their knowledge and understanding of excavation and trenching operations may also enroll in this safety training course.

There are no prerequisites for this course.

It is up to the employer to determine the employee's capabilities and to designate trained and knowledgeable persons.

overview: The OSHA Welding, Cutting, and Brazing for Construction Training is designed to provide workers in the construction industry with the necessary awareness-level knowledge to safely perform welding, cutting, and brazing operations. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) has specific regulations and guidelines in place to protect workers from hazards associated with welding, cutting or brazing.

The training is intended to familiarize learners with the hazards and risks involved in these operations, such as toxic fumes, burns, electrical hazards, and eye injuries. The training emphasizes the proper selection and use of personal protective equipment (PPE) like welding helmets, gloves, goggles, and protective clothing. Workers are also trained in safe operations, inspection, and maintenance of equipment, including handling, storing gas cylinders, and correctly using welding machines and torches. Fire safety measures are covered, such as understanding flammability, using fire extinguishers, and implementing fire watch procedures. Proper ventilation techniques to control exposure to hazardous fumes and gases are taught. The training highlights safe work practices like maintaining a clean work area, securing workpieces, and following proper procedures for equipment operation and storage.

Welding, Cutting, and Brazing are addressed in specific OSHA standards for the general industry (29 CFR 1910 Subparts I, Q, and Z), construction industry (29 CFR 1926 Subparts J and Z), and maritime (29 CFR 1915 Subpart D, I, G, P, and Z).

What is a struck-by hazard?

Any incident in which a worker is hit by a moving object, tool, vehicle, machine, or other equipment is classified as a struck-by injury. The majority of struck-by injuries involve traffic or moving vehicles. This category includes impacts with everything from falling bricks and rocks kicked up by landscaping equipment to runaway vehicles or loads swinging from a crane.
Why is the OSHA Focus Four Struck-By Hazards Prevention for Construction Training important?

- Struck-by hazards are the second-leading cause of construction deaths, after falls.

- Real OSHA investigations show workers were struck doing routine tasks such as inspecting a crane, walking near an excavator, flagging traffic.

- Struck-by claims cost the industry over $1.4 billion a year in workers' compensation.

- Vehicle-related struck-by claims average over $91,000 each, one of the most expensive injury categories.

- "Be careful around equipment" isn't training; workers need to know the 4 hazard types, the OSHA standards behind them, and the specific practice that prevents each one

This training is designed for construction workers and other personnel who may be exposed to struck-by hazards on construction sites. It may also benefit supervisors, foremen, and other personnel responsible for identifying and controlling construction-site hazards.

overview: Road construction sites are some of the most dangerous places to work in the country. With all the machinery running alongside active traffic, one mistake can lead to a disaster. This may sound like common sense, but the fact is that no worksite operates without a flagger at the heart of it. Construction sites rely on them, crews trust them, and people count on them without even knowing it.

This certification training is based on key regulations, Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) Standards 23 CFR Part 655 Subpart F, the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) Chapter 6E Section 6D.05/6E. and OSHA Construction Industry Standards 29 CFR 1926 Subpart G, and ANSI/ISEA 107-2020 High-visibility Apparel Standards.

They do more than signal traffic; they manage risks, establish order amid chaos, and make life-saving decisions that affect the lives of workers behind the barrier and motorists ahead of it.

Yes, construction industry fire regulations mirror the general industry standards this course is built on, so the guidance applies equally on a construction site.
Why is the incipient fire stage training important?

Fire safety training isn’t just a best practice; it’s a core requirement for protecting workers, assets, and day-to-day operations in industrial environments. Effective training helps employees understand risks, respond quickly to emergencies, and reduce the severity of fire-related incidents.

Below are some of the most important reasons fire safety training is essential for industrial workers:

- Protecting Lives and Reducing Injuries

- Preventing Property Damage and Business Disruption

- Meeting OSHA, NFPA, and Local Fire Code Requirements

- Fire safety requirements

- Supporting Productivity and Operational Continuity

- Employees working in offices and commercial facilities

- Construction and maintenance workers

- Facilities and building maintenance personnel

- Laboratory and research personnel

Do I need to fight every fire I see?

No. This course exists precisely because that's the wrong instinct. Fighting a fire is only appropriate when it's still in the incipient stage — small, confined to its point of origin, and controllable with a single extinguisher. Anything beyond that, and the right move is to evacuate.
Is fire extinguisher training required for employees?

Yes, OSHA requires hands-on training before an employee first uses one, not just a walkthrough, because muscle memory under stress is different from watching someone else do it once. Make sure you provide hands-on training for your employees through live-fire training props.
Does every employee need to take this course?

No. Employers can authorize only certain employees to use extinguishers and require everyone else to evacuate, and if they do, they're exempt from some of the extinguisher distribution requirements that otherwise apply.

faqs: What is Workplace Violence?

Workplace violence is any act or threat of physical violence, harassment, intimidation, or other disruptive behavior that occurs at the worksite. It includes verbal abuse, threats, physical assault, and homicide, and may involve employees, customers, clients, or visitors. It can occur inside the workplace or in work-related settings outside of it.
What are the four types of workplace violence?

Workplace violence is typically categorized into four types: Type 1 (criminal intent — perpetrator has no relationship to the workplace), Type 2 (customer/client violence), Type 3 (worker-on-worker violence), and Type 4 (personal relationship violence that spills into the workplace). Understanding each type helps organizations tailor their prevention strategies appropriately.

An effective Workplace Violence Prevention Program includes a written policy statement, a worksite analysis and hazard assessment, specific prevention and control measures, a clear incident reporting and investigation process, post-incident response procedures, and documented employee training. OSHA recommends these elements as part of a comprehensive program under the General Duty Clause.

faqs: What is a confined space?

A confined space is an area with limited access that is not designed for continuous human occupancy. Workers may need to enter these spaces to perform specific job tasks. Examples include tanks, ducts, crawl spaces, manholes, attics, turbines, and drilled shafts.

According to OSHA, a space is considered confined if it meets three criteria:

- It is large enough and configured so an employee can fully enter it.

- It has limited or restricted means of entry and exit.

- It is not designed for continuous occupancy.

overview: Confined spaces can be extremely hazardous. This Permit-Required Confined Space Training for construction and general industry workers ensures that they understand OSHA requirements for entering permit spaces to make informed decisions.

overview: Welding, cutting, brazing, and grinding are routine tasks in manufacturing plants, fabrication shops, and industrial maintenance operations, but hot work is also one of the leading causes of workplace fires when permits, fire watches, or basic precautions are skipped.

The course is based on OSHA 29 CFR 1910 Subpart Q—Welding, Cutting and Brazing and incorporates industry best practices from the NFPA 51B, Standard for Fire Prevention During Welding, Cutting, and Other Hot Work. Participants will learn about regulatory requirements, fire prevention, hot work permits, hazard assessments, personal protective equipment (PPE), emergency response procedures, and safe work practices that help prevent injuries, property damage, and workplace fires.
audience: Employees who perform welding, cutting, brazing, soldering, or other hot work
Maintenance and repair personnel
Production and manufacturing workers
Supervisors and managers responsible for hot work activities
Employees who authorize, plan, or oversee hot work
Fire watch personnel
Safety professionals and workplace safety coordinators
Contractors performing hot work in general industry facilities

syllabus.intro: This OSHA Hot Work Safety for General Industry Training consists of 5 lessons. Students are required to take each lesson in sequential order as listed below.

modules.title: Lesson 1: Introduction and Regulatory Requirements
modules.desc: This lesson establishes the foundation for hot work safety by defining hot work, introducing common hot work activities, and explaining the OSHA requirements and applicable industry standards that govern these operations. It also highlights the responsibilities of employers and employees and the serious consequences that can result from unsafe hot work.

modules.title: Lesson 2: Hot Work Hazards
modules.desc: This lesson examines the major hazards associated with hot work, including fire, explosions, electrical energy, burns, hazardous atmospheres, compressed gases, and combustible materials. It emphasizes the importance of evaluating facility conditions and planning appropriate controls before work begins.

modules.title: Lesson 3: Additional Hot Work Hazards and Risk Assessment
modules.desc: This lesson focuses on less visible but potentially serious hazards associated with hot work, including toxic fumes, metal exposure, radiation, and hazardous welding byproducts. It also introduces the hierarchy of controls and explains how hazard assessments and pre-job planning help determine effective measures to eliminate or reduce risk.

modules.title: Lesson 4: Safe Hot Work Practices and Fire Prevention
modules.desc: This lesson explains how to conduct hot work safely through effective planning, equipment checks, fire prevention measures, appropriate PPE, ventilation, and control of sparks and slag. It also emphasizes protecting nearby workers and maintaining safe conditions throughout the operation.

modules.title: Lesson 5: Emergency Procedures and Incident Prevention
modules.desc: This lesson prepares workers to respond appropriately to fires, equipment failures, and other hot work emergencies. It also covers incident reporting, evacuation, post-work fire monitoring, and using lessons learned to prevent similar incidents in the future.

objectives: Define hot work and identify common hot work activities performed in warehouses and facilities.
Recognize the fire, explosion, electrical, burn, and health hazards associated with hot work operations.
Identify OSHA requirements and industry best practices governing hot work safety in facilities.
Explain the roles and responsibilities of employers and employees in maintaining hot work safety.
Identify hazardous materials, combustible conditions, and other factors that increase hot work risks.
Apply safe work practices for welding, cutting, grinding, brazing, soldering, and related hot work activities.
Recognize the health hazards associated with welding fumes, toxic gases, and radiation exposure, and identify appropriate control measures.
Select appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) and engineering controls for hot work operations.
Conduct basic pre-job planning and site-specific hazard assessments before performing hot work.
Identify proper fire prevention measures, including fire watches, hot work permits, and post-work fire monitoring.
Choose the appropriate portable fire extinguisher for different classes of fire and apply safe fire response practices.
Demonstrate appropriate emergency response procedures, including evacuation, incident reporting, and response to equipment failures.
faqs: Which federal OSHA standards are covered by the OSHA Hot Work Safety for General Industry?
This course meets and exceeds the compliance requirements outlined in OSHA Standard 29 CFR 1910.252 — Welding, Cutting, and Brazing (General Requirements), part of 1910 Subpart Q.
Why is the Hot Work Training for General Industry important?

Hot work is one of the leading causes of industrial fires, and most incidents trace back to skipped permits, missing fire watches, or uncontrolled ignition sources near combustibles. This training closes that gap for personnel who weld, cut, braze, or grind in general industry settings.
What makes construction hot work different from the general industry hot work?

Construction sites change daily, combustible materials arrive and accumulate, buildings have open floors and walls that allow sparks to fall freely, multiple trades work simultaneously without always knowing what others are doing nearby, and permanent fire protection systems are typically not yet installed. This course addresses the specific OSHA construction standard (29 CFR 1926 Subpart J) and the unique precautions that the dynamic environment requires, including gas cylinder handling and preservative coating requirements that don’t exist in the general industry standard.
Who would benefit from enrolling in the Hot Work Certification for the General Industry?

This training is suitable for:

- Employees who perform welding, cutting, brazing, soldering, or other hot work

- Maintenance and repair personnel

- Production and manufacturing workers

- Supervisors and managers responsible for hot work activities

- Employees who authorize, plan, or oversee hot work

- Fire watch personnel

- Safety professionals and workplace safety coordinators

- Contractors performing hot work in general industry facilities

The course is particularly relevant to manufacturing plants, warehouses, maintenance facilities, utilities, industrial operations, and other general industry workplaces where hot work activities may create fire or other safety hazards.
Example work sites this Hot Work training can be used on?

Manufacturing plants, fabrication and machine shops, industrial maintenance departments, warehouses and distribution centers, food and beverage processing facilities, and vehicle or heavy-equipment repair shops.
Are there any prerequisites for enrolling in course for Hot Work Safety Training?
There are no prerequisites for this course.
Is a refresher training required for the Hot Work Certification?

OSHA's hot work standard does not specify a set frequency for training renewal, unlike some other OSHA regulations. However, industry best practices suggest providing Hot Work safety Training at least once a year.
Will I receive my OSHA Hot Work Safety for General Industry Online Training certificate? When will it expire, and what is its validity?

Certificate of Completion: Immediately after passing the final exam, you can download, save, or print your certificate in PDF format.

Validity: The course certificate is valid for two year.

Renewal: Simply take this course in 24 months to maintain compliance and stay current on hot work best practices at facilities.

This course gives industry-specific knowledge on the types of gases, types of cylinders, potential hazards, safety inspections, installation, storage, transportation, as well as safe operating practices, such as leak tests and safe operation of valves, regulators, and controls.

Incidents involving compressed gases continue to cause serious workplace injuries due to fires, explosions, asphyxiation, and uncontrolled releases of pressure. Proper training helps reduce these risks, strengthens OSHA compliance, and protects workers, facilities, and equipment from potentially catastrophic events.

faqs: What are Compressed Gas Cylinders?

Compression gas cylinders are strong, sealed containers specifically built to store gases under high pressure. These cylinders are manufactured in such a way that they can withstand internal pressure and are able to safely contain gases, which may be compressed, liquefied, or dissolved.
Why is the OSHA Compressed Gas Cylinders Safety Training course important?

This Compressed Gas Safety Program Training is important as it:

- Assists in safe handling, using, and working around compressed gas cylinders.

- Protects against the dangers that might arise from leaks, fire, explosion, asphyxiation, and mechanical failure of cylinders.

- Develops skills necessary to conduct a proper pre-use check and identify cylinders that are damaged, leaking, or installed improperly.

- Instructs on how to operate, store, and transport cylinders to avoid tipping, valve damage, and unplanned gas releases.

- Helps users comply with OSHA regulations and safe practices when working with compressed gas cylinders.
Which federal OSHA standards are covered by the OSHA Compressed Gas Cylinder Safety Training?

This course meets and exceeds the compliance requirements outlined in OSHA Standards 29 CFR 1910.101, 29 CFR 1910.102, 29 CFR 1910.103, 29 CFR 1910.104, 29 CFR 1910.105, 29 CFR 1910.253, and 29 CFR 1926.350.
Which other standards are covered by this OSHA Cylinder Hazard Safety Training?

This Compressed Gas Cylinder Safety Training also covers NFPA 51, NFPA 55, and NFPA 99. Similarly, it also covers Department of Transportation (DOT) 49 CFR 171, 49 CFR 172, 49 CFR 173 Subpart G, 49 CFR 178 Subpart C, and 49 CFR 180 Subpart C.

There are no prerequisites for this course.

Employees who handle or work with compressed gas cylinders should receive refresher training every three years to maintain safe work practices. Refresher training is recommended when:

faqs: What is the most common cause of flammable liquid incidents?
Failure to control ignition sources, improper storage, and a lack of understanding of vapor behavior are the leading causes that this course will cover.
Why is the Flammable and Combustible Liquids Awareness course important?

When flammable liquids are involved, only trained professionals or workers should do the work. Because risks are high, an untrained person can cause a serious fire and be stuck in a life-or-death situation. Even a small mistake, such as the one mentioned below, can lead to catastrophic incidents such as the following:

- improper storage

- incorrect labeling

- poor ventilation

- static electricity discharge

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.106 and NFPA 30 require employees to understand the properties of flammable liquids, recognize ignition sources, and follow safe handling practices to prevent accidents.

overview: Atmospheric hazards rarely give any warning. A tank that "looked fine" turns out to be oxygen-deficient. A meter that wasn't bump-tested that morning misses a flammable vapor.

A hot work permit covers the task area, but not the connected piping where gas actually migrates in from. Every one of those moments is exactly where this course matters. Workers and technicians need to test the air and recognize atmospheric hazards before it matters, not after. They should check if portable gas detectors are calibrated and running as expected in:

OSHA Air Monitoring & Gas Detection Training provides workers with this knowledge. The course covers key OSHA requirements, including OSHA’s General Duty Clause, 29 CFR 1910.1000 – Air Contaminants, 29 CFR 1926.65 and 29 CFR 1910.120 – Hazardous Waste Operations and Emergency Response (HAZWOPER), 29 CFR 1910.146 – Permit-Required Confined Spaces, 29 CFR 1926.1203 – General Requirements for Construction Confined Spaces, and 29 CFR 1926.1204 – Permit-Required Confined Spaces.

faqs: Which federal OSHA standards are covered by the OSHA Air Monitoring and Gas Detection Training?

The course covers key OSHA requirements, including OSHA’s General Duty Clause, 29 CFR 1910.1000 – Air Contaminants, 29 CFR 1926.65 and 29 CFR 1910.120 – Hazardous Waste Operations and Emergency Response (HAZWOPER), 29 CFR 1910.146 – Permit-Required Confined Spaces, 29 CFR 1926.1203 – General Requirements for Construction Confined Spaces, and 29 CFR 1926.1204 – Permit-Required Confined Spaces.
Why is the OSHA Air Monitoring and Gas Detection Training important?

Atmospheric hazards can't be seen, smelled, or felt until it's too late. The only way to catch them is by testing the air before and during the work. This course teaches workers and technicians how to do that correctly: recognize hazards, use gas detectors properly, and know when to test, retest, and hold off on entry. Get it wrong, and a routine task turns into a fatality. Get it right, and it's just another safe day on the job.
Who would benefit from enrolling in the OSHA Air Monitoring and Gas Detection Training?

This training is suitable for workers and supervisors whose jobs may involve hazardous atmospheres or areas where gas detection and air monitoring are required, including:

- Confined-space entrants

- Gas detection technicians

- Entry supervisors

- Gas testers and atmospheric monitoring personnel

- Maintenance and industrial workers

Important: This course covers air monitoring and gas detection principles and safe work practices. It does not, by itself, authorize a worker to perform duties that require additional employer-specific qualification, competency evaluation, or certification.
Is this the same as confined space entry training?

No, confined space entry (attendant/entrant/supervisor duties) is a separate topic. This course focuses specifically on atmospheric hazard recognition and gas detection equipment, which applies across confined space, hot work, and routine maintenance settings.
What's the difference between a bump test and a calibration, and does the course cover both?

Yes, this is one of the most commonly confused points in the field, and a full lesson covers it. A bump test confirms the sensors respond; it doesn't verify accuracy. Calibration adjusts the instrument against a known gas standard.

overview: This course is designed for workers potentially exposed to hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) in the workplace. In accordance with OSHA’s General Duty Clause and ANSI/ASSP Z390.1-2017 which sets forth accepted practices for hydrogen sulfide training programs.

Hydrogen sulfide (H 2 S) is a colorless, highly flammable, and extremely hazardous gas with a characteristic, pungent “rotten egg” odor. Hydrogen sulfide is produced naturally by decaying organic matter and is released from sludge, liquid manure, sulfur hot springs, and natural gas.

It is used in several industrial processes and is produced as a by-product during oil refining, mining, and rayon manufacturing. Hydrogen sulfide is a highly toxic substance; therefore, adequate training and knowledge are of prime importance when working with or around sources of hydrogen sulfide.

According to the U.S. Chemical Safety Board, hydrogen sulfide exposure has caused thousands of workplace injuries and fatalities. The industrial sectors over the past decades, specifically highlights the critical need for effective hydrogen sulfide awareness training.
This OSHA Hydrogen Sulfide Awareness Training course equips workers with knowledge about H₂S properties, health risks, and safe practices to minimize exposure.

How are OSHA’s standards on electrical safety and NFPA 70E 2024 standards related to workplace safety?

The NFPA 70E is an internationally accepted American National Standard that defines electrical safety-related work practices.

The U.S. Department of Labor’s Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) looks to the prescriptive-based requirements of NFPA 70E to fulfill the performance-based requirements included in its standards.

NFPA 70E elaborates on how the performance-based requirements in OSHA’s standards can be met by providing and defining minimum standard industry practices necessary for electrical safety.

OSHA is the law, and NFPA 70E outlines ways to comply with OSHA’s electrical safety training requirements.

This symbiotic relationship between NFPA 70E and OSHA electrical safety standards helps to increase safety in the workplace.
What is the employer's role after the Electrical Safety Training is complete?

After the training is complete, the employer must audit the company’s electrical safety program every three years to verify that employees are following the safety-related work practices required by 2024 NFPA 70E requirements.

In alignment with this standard, HAZWOPER OSHA Training, LLC also updates this course every three years to ensure it reflects the most current regulatory requirements and industry best practices.
Can the NFPA 70E guidelines be used worldwide?

The NFPA 70E is an internationally applied standard. The electrical safety-related work practices, safety-related maintenance requirements, and other administrative controls in NFPA 70E apply to all alternating and direct current systems. The requirements in NFPA 70E standard for electrical safety in the workplace 2024 applies to all types of employees, employers, and facilities, including in-house employees, contract employees, contractor employees, general industrial workplaces, and construction workplaces, regardless of their location in the United States and its territories.
Is NFPA 70E mandatory?

Following NFPA 70E is not a legal requirement in most cases. However, OSHA requires employers to protect employees from electrical hazards. Since NFPA 70E is the industry-recognized consensus standard for doing so, following it is the best way to meet OSHA requirements.

What is the difference between a GFCI and a regular circuit breaker?

A standard circuit breaker protects equipment and wiring from overloads and short circuits. A GFCI protects people by detecting small current imbalances (ground faults) and shutting off power within milliseconds to reduce the risk of electric shock.
Does a GFCI protect against all electrical hazards?
No. A GFCI protects against ground-fault shock hazards.

There are no prerequisites for this course.

- Job duties change,

overview: OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Training course is designed to provide a basic understanding of OSHA’s Bloodborne Pathogens Standard 29 CFR 1910.1030, its scope, bloodborne diseases, their modes of transmission and prevention, and other pertinent information.

Bloodborne pathogens are infectious microorganisms in human blood that can cause disease in humans. These pathogens are transmitted from one infected individual to another through blood and other potentially infectious materials (OPIM). These pathogens include (but are not limited to) hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).

OSHA’s bloodborne pathogens standard prescribes guidelines and safeguards to protect workers who are exposed to health hazards related to bloodborne pathogens. Furthermore, the Needlestick Safety and Prevention Act of 2000 modified OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens standard by requiring employers to identify, evaluate, and implement safer medical devices, such as needleless systems and sharps with engineered sharps protections. The Act also mandated additional requirements for maintaining a sharps injury log and for the involvement of non-managerial healthcare workers in identifying, evaluating, and choosing effective engineering and work practice controls.
audience: Healthcare personnel, nurses, doctors, and medical assistants, as well as first responders such as EMTs, paramedics, firefighters, and law enforcement officers.
Housekeeping, janitorial, and laundry staff in hospitals, clinics, or other facilities also need training to safely handle contaminated materials.
Laboratory workers, researchers, and students who work with blood or OPIM require proper safety knowledge to prevent accidental exposures.
Professionals in tattoo, piercing, cosmetology, construction, maintenance, and utility work may encounter blood on the job and must know safe practices.
Volunteers, community care workers, and staff in educational or childcare settings also benefit from this training to protect themselves and others.
